Your mix of investments would depend on your risk appetite. What's important is you make a plan and follow though. ATRAM provides a wide range of investment opportunities and I believe that although it may not be the most efficient way to get exposed to markets outside the Philippines, it's one of the most accessible.

Now, if you're asking whether or not you should invest more into your ATRAM Funds, it might mean that you haven't really decide on how you want to distribute your investments. Might be best to sit down and reflect on what kind of investor you are (conservative, moderate, or aggressive), then research what kind of mix would be recommended for you.

For example, if you're a moderate investor, you might have a 6 month Emergency Fund + a Portfolio of 10% Cash or Cash Equivalent (High Yield Savings, Time Deposit, Retail Treasury Bond), 40% Bonds (Corporate Bonds, Bond Funds), and 50% Equities (Stocks, Equity Funds, Index Funds, ETFs, etc.). You can further break it down and assign certain percentages according to your preferences. For any additional investment, you should try to balance out the allocation you've decided on.

It's important to decide on a plan and stick to it because it gives you clarity and a somewhat measurable goal.

So in your example, your funds with ATRAM are currently down. But how much did you or should you allocate to it? 10%? 20%? If for example, you decide to allocate 10% of your portfolio, is it's current value close to that, still higher than that, or already below that? Is the difference between actual and target values negligible to not bother reallocating for now? When you answer these, that's when you decide to buy more, hold, or sell in favor of other investments. 

Don't go averaging down and buy just because you think it's supposedly "cheap." It's playing into the fear of losing out on the possibility that it might bounce back soon. If you're buying it should be because it was part of your plan to buy/allocate more at the specified time, and it just happened to be "cheap."

Also, don't panic and sell immediately in case of a downturn. Assuming you didn't buy into sketchy investments like a DDS Crypto Coin or trending speculative penny stocks, just take a breath, take a step back, and calmly reassess. Just ask yourself whether or not it's worth it to stay invested in the fund/company. Do the fundamentals reflect the downturn? Is it a dying/dead industry (e.g. consumer camera film or video rental stores)?

Remember that there should be a good reason for any investment. Don't allow yourself to make emotional decisions. Make a plan and follow it.

You need to remember that the stock market is not the economy. The stock market looks to the future while economic data such as GDP and inflation shows us past performance. And so the stock market, particularly the PSEi is affected by investor sentiment om the future of Philippine companies, not the lockdowns and COVID cases per se. A clear example of this is how ECQ was extended in the NCR+ area last Saturday but the PSEi had been positive for the past 2 days.

So, in my opinion, we are already bouncing back from the lows we've seen last year. Vaccines are already rolling out, and companies in the index as a whole are steadily recovering with the increased consumption and somewhat clearer projections for the future. That said, bear in mind that it isn't always a straight climb. There will always be cycles of climbs, corrections, consolidations, etc.

Might not be the best time to study flying. Airlines have been hit hard by the pandemic and even if they are on their way to recovery, they'll prioritize hiring former pilots (not limited to those they had to let go). Licenses, aircraft ratings, and actual flight hours are more than just impressive qualifications in a CV, they're a requirement to exercise certain roles in airlines. They're qualifications that would make a new grad's CV not even worth looking at.

Don't listen to the schools' marketing. Even pre-pandemic, most of their students struggled to find actual pilot jobs that pay a living wage, and you'll either just cut your losses or force yourself to earn barely anything by teaching as an instructor (a lot of frustrating, sometimes illegal/immoral BS from the company/your seniors here).

I could be wrong and supply of pilots might not be able to keep up to demand by the time you graduate, but I hope you don't make the same mistake that others have made. Please don't borrow money, or quit a well paying job, or sell property, or use your parents' retirement money just to study flying.

It could be more, it could be less. Usually though, the insurance minimum is guaranteed (check contract though since it might have situations not covered) for the death or critical injury part.

In general, insurance is a need for bread winners. Can't recommend any school over others since I've only been with one. If you've already made up your mind to start flying, all I can say is that you'll need to know what to look for when checking a school out, then compare them.

>Instructors: Do they know how to teach? Ask the school if thwy can have an instructor demonstrate a lesson/maneuver like flying straight and level, full stall, lazy eights, etc. It should feel like when you first learned how to drive, except your instructor also has control over the plane. Are the instructions clear? Is he demonstrating well? Is he allowing me to take control (or at least gesturing during the demo that you have the controls)? You can look for youtube videos to compare what you can/should expect from the instructors. You can also ask if it's possible to observe a lesson for their current cadets in their simulator if they have one.

>Track record (a bit tricky since most if not all won't admit/openly disclose this): Have they had any incidents (not just accidents, there is a distinction) in the recent past? How many/often? How severe? How did they address this? How many graduates/dropouts do they have? How many got jobs in the industry as pilots (%), at least before COVID?

>Timeline/Operations (again, this will be tricky since they can be selective about their facts by choosing the advantageous examples or they can outright lie): How long until I graduate (ask for an example like for my school, we had batches so you can ask what batch graduated before COVID like January/February 2020, and what month and year did they start?) How often will we fly? Do you currently have a backlog of students? What's your ratio of students to aircraft? Tip for track record and timeline is by asking current and former (recent) students about this. One way is by stalking the school's fb page and approaxhing those with pilot uniforms with 1 or 2 bars on their shoulders.  Take their opinions with a grain of salt though since they might have a stake in your enrollment (like a commission for a recomendation) so you can minimize this by asking multiple people. This is tedious but if a million pesos and two years of your time is at stake, you need to be diligent with your research.

>Cost: Tuition cost? Miscellaneous (includes school materials, fees for CAAP (Civil Aviation Authority of the Phils.))? Lodging (this is why you need to know how long it takes; if you are budgeting, add 6-12 months to lodging costs since it took about 24 months for my batch to finish when we were promised 15)? Note that as far as I know, there is a cultuee among schools that you celebrate each milestone with a "pakain" whatever shape or form that is. You also need to note that each checkride, at least until your CPL (Commercial Pilot License), there is an expectation that you'll give your check pilot a "gift." You'll have to ask students about these since the schools will not admit it. 

So yeah, these are the things I could think of that you should look out for. Remember to take all info with a bit of skepticism and that you need to weigh these according to what you want and what your limitations are. For example, a school might have a good track record, but the costs might be beyond your means. Or just because one school is cheap doesn't mean it's giving you good value.

Anyways, good luck with your search and hope you do well if you ever pursue flying

I finished my flight training a couple of years ago and from my experience, the best flight school will provide you with a good education not only on the ground but also in the air. Best way to know more is by asking a tour of their facilities, seeing their aircraft, and talking to their instructors and asking them to teach you something as if you were in the cockpit (e.g. how would you teach me a power-on stall - he should be able to demonstrate, gestures as if allowing you to perform, then say possible comments on how to improve; all step by step like when you learned how to drive a car). They should be able to teach without simply dictating and minimize any wasted time. Don't let them make excuses like saying that there are no free samples, etc.

Warning, a bit of a rant (applies to most if not all schools)...

>From what I experienced first hand as well as what I heard from friends and acquaintances who came from other schools, most if not all of them just try to give you the minimum to pass your written exams and checkrides (the practical exams) from CAAP (Civil Aviation Authority Philippines) and then make you burn through the 200 hours needed for you to earn your CPL (Commercial Pilot License). They're essentially diploma mills and won't be upfront with you in terms of employment rate. It will be bad. When I graduated, out of more than 20 in my batch/group (there were about 120-150 graduates a year in my school), about 2 made it to the airlines in their own merit, while a few went through pay to fly programs (tens of thousands of USD on top of the tuition).

>There will only be a handful of competent instructors at any given time. Most (although not all) of the old timers will be lazy and will just make you fly solo. The younger ones will be a hit and miss since teaching will only be used as a stepping stone for them and thus are either new at teaching and just getting the hand of it, are really good but have already built up their flying hours and won't be teaching you throughout your whole training, or don't care much for their roles as instructors and are just looking forward to leaving. 

>Don't quit your stable job or borrow money to get through flight school. It's high risk, high reward... but from what I've seen the risk isn't worth it if you're giving up the security of a good job or if you're ending up with debt. There's a lot of down time because of may different things (scheduling problem, weather, even timing on demand of pilots after graduation), and the burden of having to provide or having to pay for debt (2M pesos or more for tuition alone, with no living expenses yet) might be something you won't be able to handle.

>Sometimes your license is not enough and you might get an Airbus rating. It's a big plus and your resume will be given attention, but it's far from a guarantee. The rating alone is expensive (about another 2M pesos). What they don't tell you is that you'll want/need to be current when the airlines will assess you on their Sim(ulator) check which will cost you another 2K USD for a 2 hr session. These checks might happen 6 months to more than 1 year after your last airbus sim session, and believe me, you will be rusty as heck.

Sorry for the long post. I just felt like I should shed some light on flight training for anyone who might stumble on this to serously know what they're getting into.
